reference.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / IDSA cryptococcosis guidance
clinicalPearls: An encapsulated environmental yeast associated with certain trees (classically eucalyptus) and soil, historically tropical/subtropical but with a recognised temperate focus in the Pacific Northwest of North America
Unlike Cryptococcus neoformans, which predominantly affects those with advanced HIV or other immunosuppression, C. gattii frequently causes disease in apparently immunocompetent hosts
It has a propensity to form space-occupying mass lesions, with pulmonary cryptococcomas and cerebral cryptococcomas that can mimic tumours
Presentations include chronic cough with lung masses and subacute meningoencephalitis with headache, cranial nerve palsies, and features of raised intracranial pressure
Neurological disease may respond more slowly than C. neoformans, with a greater need for surgical management of large mass lesions and aggressive control of intracranial pressure
Treatment follows an induction, consolidation, and maintenance strategy using amphotericin-based and azole antifungal agents, with repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures to manage raised pressure
Diagnosis uses cryptococcal antigen testing (serum and cerebrospinal fluid), India ink microscopy, culture, and neuroimaging to define cryptococcomas
reference.pathophysiology: Cryptococcus gattii is acquired by inhaling infectious propagules from environmental sources associated with trees and soil. The yeast's polysaccharide capsule is a key virulence factor that impairs phagocytosis and modulates the immune response. After a pulmonary portal of entry the organism can disseminate haematogenously with a strong neurotropism, seeding the central nervous system. In contrast to C. neoformans, C. gattii tends to elicit a granulomatous response and to form discrete mass lesions (cryptococcomas) in the lung and brain, and it is capable of causing significant disease in hosts with no identifiable immune defect.
additionalDifferentials: Primary or metastatic lung or brain tumours
Other endemic mycoses such as histoplasmosis or coccidioidomycosis
additionalInvestigations: Cryptococcal antigen testing on serum and cerebrospinal fluid
India ink microscopy and fungal culture of cerebrospinal fluid
Lumbar puncture with measurement of opening pressure
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain to identify cryptococcomas and hydrocephalus
Computed tomography of the chest to characterise pulmonary nodules or masses
Species identification to distinguish C. gattii from C. neoformans and HIV testing to assess immune status
redFlags: Features of markedly raised intracranial pressure such as reduced consciousness, papilloedema, or cranial nerve palsies
Large cerebral cryptococcomas causing mass effect
Progressive neurological deficit despite antifungal therapy
Respiratory compromise from extensive pulmonary disease
reference.prognosis: With prompt antifungal therapy and diligent control of intracranial pressure many patients recover, but large cryptococcomas respond slowly, neurological sequelae can occur, and disease in immunocompetent hosts may still be protracted and require prolonged treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming cryptococcosis only occurs in immunocompromised patients and dismissing it in an immunocompetent host
Mistaking pulmonary or cerebral cryptococcomas for malignancy
Neglecting management of raised intracranial pressure, a major driver of morbidity
Failing to distinguish C. gattii from C. neoformans, which affects expected course and management
Underestimating the prolonged treatment and possible surgery needed for large mass lesions
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
IDSA clinical practice guidelines for the management of cryptococcal disease
